How did London get here (Families in London temporary housing told they cannot use in-built air conditioning, 27 July)? Your report says homeless families, including young children, were placed in a glass tower during a heatwave and told they could not use the building’s air conditioning because it had “not been offered as an amenity”. If that doesn’t make every Londoner stop in disbelief, we’ve become dangerously desensitised. This is no longer a housing crisis, it is a crisis of basic human dignity.
London proudly markets itself as one of the world’s greatest cities: a global financial capital overflowing with luxury developments, billion-pound property portfolios and record-breaking real estate values. Yet, in the shadow of that wealth, children are being expected to endure dangerously hot flats where the very system designed to make the building habitable is effectively treated as a luxury.
When a city reaches the point where vulnerable families are housed in buildings that become ovens, while the solution exists but is deemed off limits, something has gone profoundly wrong.
This isn’t an administrative oversight. It is the triumph of bureaucracy over common sense and, ultimately, over compassion. Politicians have spent years telling us London is thriving. Thriving for whom? It certainly isn’t thriving for the record number of families trapped in temporary accommodation or the children growing up without a stable home.
History teaches us that great cities are judged not by the height of their skyscrapers, but by how they treat those with the least power. On that measure, London should be deeply ashamed. A city where air conditioning exists but compassion is switched off is no longer a world-class city. It is simply a dystopia.
Fernando Quintana Marrero
London

German official defends deportation of non-criminal to Afghanistan
The German government on Wednesday defended its decision to deport an Afghan back to their homeland despite not being convicted of any crime.
On Tuesday evening, the latest in a series of deportation flights from Germany to Afghanistan took off, carrying 31 Afghan people.
But unlike previous flights, which saw only criminals deported to the Taliban-run country, Tuesday's flight was the first to include a person not convicted of a crime.
On Tuesday, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said that those on the latest flight were mostly "serious offenders who had committed crimes such as murder, rape and acts of violence," but admitted that "the designation of 'convicted offender' does not apply" to one of the passengers on board.
The government has said that it prioritizes deporting individuals convicted of serious crimes.
An Interior Ministry spokesperson told reporters on Wednesday that the government aimed to "begin with deporting people who have been convicted and those who pose a threat" but that it was also possible "to put people on deportation flights who are not criminals."
Dobrindt said on Tuesday that "people who have no right to stay in the country can also be subject to deportation if there are no signs they have integrated in Germany."
As a member of Chancellor Merz's conservative party, Dobrindt defended the government's actions and said it would continue to pursue a strict immigration policy with a "firm stance."
Refugee rights groups sharply criticized the deportation, and Tuesday's flight, which set off from Leipzig, was accompanied by protests of about 250 people, according to officials.
Germany bakes, as another heatwave sweeps the country
Temperatures rose to 38 degrees Celsius (100 degrees Fahrenheit) in some parts of western and southwestern Germany on Wednesday, as the high-pressure system "Olaf" makes the country sweat.
And yet, peak temperatures will likely only be reached on Thursday, when the heat is expected to reach as high as 39 C (102 F) in some areas of Germany, according to the German Meteorological Service (DWD).
Heavy rain and thunderstorms are forecasted to follow the heat, with hurricane-force wind gusts possible in northern Germany.
The recent heatwave comes just weeks after Germany faced an early summer heatwave in June, which broke temperature records, with a high of 41.8 C (107 F) recorded in the state of Saxony-Anhalt.
The June heatwave is believed to have caused over 5,100 excess deaths in Germany alone, with thousands of others in neighboring European countries.
Thorsten Frei confirmed as conservative parliamentary faction chief
Thorsten Frei was confirmed as the parliamentary faction chief of the conservative bloc on Wednesday afternoon.
In a vote at a special session of lawmakers from the governing CDU and CSU parties, Frei received 91.9% of the vote.
Frei, a close confidant of Friedrich Merz, previously served as the chancellor's chief of staff. He replaces Jens Spahn, who stepped down as faction chief this month after it became known that he and his partner had a child via surrogacy, a practice that is prohibited in Germany and which Spahn himself had spoken out against in the past.
The infighting in the conservative bloc hit Merz at a time his popularity among Germans is low, the economy is stagnating and the far-right populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) is topping the surveys ahead of regional elections.
"We must all reflect together on what we need to do better ... and how we can regain the trust of those who do not trust us today," Merz said after a private meeting with lawmakers from the CDU/CSU bloc.
German Cabinet backs AI-assisted processing of asylum applications
Germany's Cabinet, led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz, approved legislation on Wednesday that would allowartificial intelligence to assist authorities in processing asylum, visa and residence permit applications.
The proposed law aims to "speed up administrative processes, enable more targeted use of resources, and facilitate a systematic evaluation of current practices."
In recent years, government agencies responsible for migration issues have faced consistently high application numbers, while staff remains limited. As a result, applicants often experience long waiting periods for decisions.
The bill aims to provide a legal framework for how government agencies can use AI to support data analysis and decision-making.
It also allows migration officials to use application data to train and test AI models. Administrators would also be permitted to analyze data from previous cases to identify patterns in decision-making, which could lead to harmonized and accelerated workflows.
The government stressed, however, that AI would only be a supporting tool for officials and that final assessments and rulings in each case would remain the responsibility of human caseworkers.
Goalkeeper Manuel Neuer says retirement 'very likely'
Bayern Munich goalkeeper Manuel Neuer said he was "very likely" to go into retirement the end of the upcoming season.
Neuer, who is 40 years old and also captain of the Bayern team, has had an accomplished career, winning 13 Bundesliga and two Champions League titles with the team.
Moreover, as goalie of the German national team, he was part of the winning squad in the 2014 World Cup in Brazil.
Neuer retired from international football after the European Championship 2024 only to temporarily come out of retirement for the 2026 World Cup, a decision that did not come without controversy.
Speaking to reporters during the training camp in Southern Bavaria, he expressed hope that the upcoming Bayern season would help overcome the frustration of Germany's poor showing at the World Cup, which ended in a Round of 32 loss to Paraguay.
Neuer also credited the Bayern team and structure for staying on.
"In perhaps 85% of cases, I would have stopped," Neuer said.
"But with this team, the staff and the coaching team, it is simply a lot of fun. We always have the chance to compete for every title and this squad is right at the highest level."
Germany reshuffles Cabinet after Spahn resignation
Germany's government has moved forward with a Cabinet reshuffle sparked by the resignation of conservative parliamentary group leader Jens Spahn.
President Frank-Walter Steinmeier formally appointed Nina Warken as head of the Federal Chancellery on Wednesday, along with Carsten Linnemann as health minister and Steffen Bilger as transport minister.
The three politicians received their certificates of appointment at a ceremony in Berlin.
Thorsten Frei, whom Warken replaces at the Chancellery, is due to be elected later on Wednesday as leader of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative parliamentary bloc.
The reshuffle comes as Merz's government struggles in opinion polls ahead of three closely watched state elections in September, where the far-right Alternative for Germany is expected to make significant gains.
Carmaking giant BMW to cut up to 8,000 jobs
BMW aims to cut up to 8,000 by the end of 2027, according to company sources. The German carmaker said the reduction would primarily target office jobs, while production line workers will be spared from cuts.
The Munich-based automaker hopes to achieve the cuts through natural staff turnover as well as a voluntary redundancy scheme. The latter would be aimed at all employees in Germany not directly involved in production, who could choose to accept severance packages in a period from October 2026 to the end of 2027.
The company currently employs 84,000 staff in Germany, and roughly 154,000 globally.
BMW is the latest German car company to announce job cuts, following similar moves by rival brands Volkswagen, Mercedes and Volkswagen-owned Audi.
Germany prestigious car industry is struggling amid stiff competition from Chinese carmakers, US tariffs, and narrower profit margins from electric cars.
BMW was long considered one of the sector's more resilient players. The planned cuts come after the company warned last month that its sales in China were falling sharply.
Lawmakers expected to endorse Merz's picks for new government ministers
After conservative parliamentary group leader Jens Spahn quit over a surrogacy scandal. Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced a series of top-level changes in the German government.
On Wednesday, members of the conservative bloc are meeting in a special session where they are expected to approve Merz's picks, including the choice of Thorsten Frei as a replacement to Spahn as the conservatives new parliamentary faction chief.
Later in the day, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier will appoint a series of new ministers. Nina Warken is to take over as the chancellery's new chief of staff, while Carsten Linneman is to become health minister, and Steffen Bilger to take over as transport minister.
Merz has faced significant backlash in his own party for replacing Transport Minister Patrick Schnieder, who hails from Rhineland Palatinate, as other conservatives from the western German state protested the move.
Under Germany's constitution, incoming ministers are required to take an official oath before parliament, the Bundestag. However, with the Bundestag currently in its summer recess, the swearing-in is expected to take place only when lawmakers return in September 9.

Amber and yellow heat health alerts have come into force as parts of the UK endure the fourth widespread heatwave of the year so far.
Temperatures are forecast to peak on Wednesday with readings as high as 35C (95F) in the hottest places.
Though the heatwave will come to a quick end for many on Thursday, well above-average temperatures in the mid- to high 20s Celsius will persist into the weekend.
On Wednesday, the Environment Agency declared an official drought for more than half of England, triggered in part by the summer's unrelenting heat and significant lack of rainfall.
How hot will it get where you live?
A plume of intense heat surging north from North Africa, and already bringing exceptionally high temperatures to parts of Iberia and France, will reach the UK on Wednesday.
Temperatures are expected to climb sharply across southern and eastern England and into parts of the Midlands, marking the peak of a short but notable heatwave.
Temperatures in these areas will range from 30-35C at their highest point on Wednesday.
Some eastern areas of Wales could also edge into heatwave criteria.
The UK Health Security Agency has issued amber heat health alerts for the East Midlands, East of England, London and the south-east from 09:00 BST on 29 July until 09:00 BST on 30 July.
The alert warns that significant impacts are likely across health and social care services due to the high temperatures, including a rise in deaths, particularly among those aged 65 and over or with health conditions.
Less severe yellow heat heat alerts have also been issued for the same period for the south-west, West Midlands, and Yorkshire and the Humber.
For much of Wales and Northern England, the three-day run of temperatures of 25C or above required to classify as a heatwave will not be met.
The same is true for Scotland and Northern Ireland where temperatures will rise closer to 20C at best.
How long will the heat last?
This time around the heat spike looks set to be brief.
The hottest conditions will be concentrated on Wednesday before a weather front moving through on Thursday will usher in fresher air, bringing a noticeable change in feel.
Temperatures are expected to fall by around 5-8C compared with Wednesday's peak.
Humidity will also ease, making it more comfortable for sleeping.
Even so, it will remain warm with temperatures still well above average, sitting in the mid- to high 20s Celsius into the weekend.
Heat to exacerbate conditions in driest regions
Drought conditions were declared by the Environment Agency on Wednesday for seven areas of England.
This includes East Anglia; Hertfordshire and the whole of London; Thames Valley; Hampshire & the Isle of Wight; Devon & Cornwall; the West Midlands and Wessex (covering Dorset, Somerset, Wiltshire, and south Gloucestershire).
Paired with the significant heat, the lack of rain means dry ground and low soil moisture levels continue to be of concern.
By Friday and into the weekend, pressure will build across the southern half of the UK prolonging the dry spell further, despite a few showers in the north.
An ongoing lack of rain means hosepipe bans are in force for millions of households and dry vegetation has provided fuel for wildfires to burn in a number of areas.
According to the Met Office, rainfall in England this month is at 4.4mm, one of the lowest levels on record - tied with June 1925 and behind only February 1891 when 3.3mm were recorded.
Wisley in Surrey has been one of the driest locations in south-east England, clocking up 42 days of no rain as of 29 July.
Rainfall levels in Wales, where drought was triggered in parts last week, are so low that July 2026 is currently the fourth driest of any month since records began.

How the latest heatwave is impacting the South East
Temperatures across the South East are expected to peak in the mid-30s Celsius (95F) as a fourth heatwave begins in the region.
The UK Health and Security Agency (UKHSA) has upgraded its heat-health alert, and the amber warning currently in place means the whole population could be at risk from hot weather.
The warning is due to be lifted on Thursday morning, while the Environment Agency confirms Kent and East Sussex to be among the areas experiencing prolonged dry weather.
So, how is the South East coping?
Some struggling
The very hot weather, and lack of rain coming with it, is impacting many sectors across the region - including nurseries.
Hayley Peacock, CEO and director of Little Barn Owls Forest and Farm School Nurseries which has a number of sites across Sussex, said the heat has been "playing havoc on our nurseries and operations over the last few weeks".
The high temperatures are also proving difficult for those who rely on the land to make a living.
Earlier this week the BBC spoke to Alan Clifton-Holt, whose farm in Romney Marsh is struggling due to having "no real meaningful rain since February".
"It has made it very difficult, we've got crops that have failed, we've got crops that are particularly low in yield," he said.
On one hand, many areas of the Wisley garden have been left without irrigation, meaning leaves are beginning to fall off.
However, RHS horticulture director Tim Upson said that crops like wild carrots were "looking great", while crape myrtles were flowering well in the heat.
An alternative view
Philip Thorley from Thorley Taverns, which owns Barnacles pub in Margate, has a different perspective.
He said: "We absolutely love the hot weather... it means we get locals coming out, we get the visitors coming down to the towns.
"We're the Mediterranean of Kent down here in Margate, so we love the hot weather."
There can be a 500% uptick in takings compared to a rainy day, he added.
The reality
The Met Office has confirmed that July has so-far seen 7% of its long-term average rainfall, falling to 1% across the south of England.
While Kent and Sussex are not officially in drought, seven other regions are - including most of Surrey, meaning there have been three droughts in the past five years.
According to Met Office chief meteorologist, Will Lang, has warned that the situation is not likely to change soon.
He said: "While there are indications of occasional unsettled spells during the first part of August, bringing the chance of rain to some locations, there is currently little sign of the widespread, sustained rainfall that would be needed to make a significant difference to the areas most affected by the dry weather."

Audio By Carbonatix
Advertising Can't Do It Alone

Across the U.S., it’s a hot summer, and electricity prices are high. Various public officials and corporate websites suggest people set their thermostats to 78 degrees Fahrenheit (25.6 degrees Celsius), or even 81 F (27.2 C), as a way to stay relatively cool without breaking the bank. But as someone who studies energy costs, I know from both personal and professional experience that it’s not that simple.
The summer after my daughter’s first birthday, she began vomiting in the middle of the night and small bumps covered her chest. I thought it was the blueberries we’d given her. My husband and I cut out acidic foods and changed her milk. At the time, we often kept our thermostat set to 79 F (26.1 C). Before becoming parents, that setting kept the summer electric bill below US$200. We would sleep without blankets and take cold showers like I had in graduate school.
Then, on a cooler night, she kept her blueberries down. After that, I lowered the hallway thermostat setting enough to get her bedroom near 74 F (23.3 C). The nighttime vomiting stopped. My experience as a parent changed how I hear universal recommendations for air conditioner settings, especially during heat waves.
There is no single thermostat setting that is right for every person or every home. And there are other easy, low-cost steps that can help keep everyone comfortable when hot weather sets in.
Air conditioning is a big help, but can be costly
Every piece of cooling equipment is different, in terms of its technical design specifications, and its age and maintenance history. And the homes these systems serve vary in terms of insulation, size, sun exposure, and local climate. So there’s not one temperature setting that’s maximally energy- and cost-efficient for every home.
It may be useful to start at 78 F (25.6 C) to keep a lid on costs, but that temperature is neither a safety threshold nor a temperature every household will find comfortable and safe. If you are uncomfortable, try lowering your thermostat one degree at a time while monitoring yourself and others in your household for any signs of heat stress.
In general, a higher thermostat setting saves energy because the air conditioner has less work to do. When it is 95 F (35 C) outside, maintaining a home at 78 F requires removing less heat than maintaining it at the average level most U.S. households seek in the summer: 72 F (22.2 C). The smaller the difference between the indoor and outdoor temperatures, the less frequently or intensely the air conditioning system has to run, thereby using less electricity.
Running an air conditioner also reduces the humidity in a home. When the air is humid, sweat evaporates less effectively. The National Weather Service has a chart that says if the temperature is above 90 F (32.2 C), and the humidity is above 60%, the air will feel like it’s above 100 F (37.8 C).
Running air conditioning may be necessary in a heat wave, but it can represent over 50% of a home’s energy usage in summer months – and a similar proportion of the resulting electricity bill.
Fortunately, there are other ways you can keep yourself and your home cool for very little money.
Keep heat out
Prevent outside heat from seeping into the building by closing curtains on sun-facing windows. Close windows and doors too, unless it is cooler outside than inside, which may happen overnight or in the early morning.
And don’t add more heat inside your home if you can avoid it. For instance, avoid using the oven during the hottest part of the day.
Combine air conditioning with air movement
The moving air from a ceiling fan or a portable fan can make temperatures feel cooler, even if the thermostat is set relatively high.
But the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention say people should only use fans to cool themselves down when indoor temperatures are below 90 F (32.2 C). This is because when the air is hotter than your skin temperature – about 90 to 94 F – a fan creates a convection oven effect, accelerating the shift of heat into the body and potentially raising your body temperature to unhealthy levels.
The thermostat isn’t in every room
Remember that a hallway thermostat may not reflect the temperature in an upstairs room, or one facing the sun. Use an inexpensive thermometer to measure temperatures in the rooms where people actually sleep or spend their time. If possible, have people stay in shaded rooms or on a lower floor, or even in one space, rather than cooling every room equally.
Cool your body as well as the rooms
A cool shower or a damp cloth can provide immediate relief, and drinking water regularly helps replace fluid lost through sweating. If you are feeling really hot, consider using ice packs to help cool your body down.
Always protect your health
There are many stories of people dying indoors because they turned off their working air conditioners during times of high heat, or because their cooling system wasn’t functioning properly.
Infants and people with certain health conditions may need to be in cooler spaces for longer periods of time than healthy adults.
Don’t be afraid to seek help
If your home’s heat makes you afraid for your health, call your local 211 resident-services hotline or search online for local cooling centers where you can spend some time in air conditioning at no charge. Even a few hours in an air-conditioned space can reduce heat risk. Splash pads and public pools are other options, as are public libraries and other government buildings, or even a restaurant, cafe or movie theater, which often have air conditioning.
Keep an eye on yourself and each other for signs of heat stress. If someone becomes dizzy, weak, intensely thirsty, nauseated, confused or unusually tired, move them to a cooler place or go to the hospital. Confusion, loss of consciousness and very high body temperature can indicate heat stroke, which is a medical emergency.
Lastly, if you need help paying your electricity bills, check in with your utility company, which may have programs for spreading out your costs over time. You may even find you’re eligible for cost subsidies. State and local governments also usually have programs that help residents insulate their homes and upgrade inefficient appliances.
The best temperature setting is the one that provides adequate cooling at costs the household can sustain. While a thermostat setting of 78 F (25.6 C) is often touted as a solution, in reality it is just one of several options. In my house, becoming a mother changed the amount I determined was necessary to spend on my summer cooling bills. I couldn’t determine the right amount of cooling from the thermostat or my electricity bill – I had to look after the people in my home.

Editorial: Stay safe in the summer heat
Published 7:00 am Wednesday, July 29, 2026
Last week was hot. Really hot.
It’s too early to tell if it will be our last sweltering stretch of summer, but according to BC Hydro the province set a new all-time summer peak electricity demand record on Tuesday and then again on Wednesday evening due to air conditioning.
Hydro, along with Island Health, also offer a number of tips to stay cool during heat waves.
Tips for those without air conditioning include using fans, and closing blinds and drapes. Open up your doors and windows when it cools down in the evening and close them again when it starts to heat up in the morning.
If your home gets too hot, head to a community centre or other public place with air conditioning.
You can spray your body down with water or wear a damp shirt, take a cool shower or bath, or sit with part of your body in the water to cool down. A day at the beach with frequent dips into the cool water can make it fun, but be sure to wear sunscreen and drink plenty of water.
Keep an eye out for overheating, heat exhaustion and heat stroke. You may feel unwell, get a headache, or feel dizzy if you’re overheating. Heat exhaustion is more severe and can see you sweat heavily, get a severe headache, muscle cramps, feel extremely thirsty, and have dark urine. For overheating and heat exhaustion you need to get yourself to a cool spot and rest to bring your body temperature down.
Heat stroke is a medical emergency requiring a call to 911. Signs include confusion, fainting, decreased consciousness, nausea, vomiting, rapid breathing, faint rapid heart rate or high body temperature.
And in the heat don’t forget your pets could be suffering too. Leave them at home during a heat event rather than taking them in a hot car.
Make sure they have fresh water and a cool place to sleep. You can freeze their food or treats to help cool them down, and if your pet is a dog or other critter that likes the water, you can get a kiddie pool they can lounge in.
You should also keep in mind that the pavement gets too hot for their paws, and you should walk them during cooler times of the day, and bring water and a dish with you.
Stay safe!

Widespread Rains likely over next two days in telangana
Metro India News | Hyderabad
Telangana is set to witness widespread rainfall over the next three days under the influence of a Deep Depression moving westwards across central India. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast light to moderate rain or thundershowers at most places across the state on Wednesday, many places on Thursday and a few places on Friday.
The IMD has also issued an Orange Alert for Day 1, warning of heavy to very heavy rainfall at isolated places in the northern and northeastern districts, including Adilabad, Komaram Bheem Asifabad, Mancherial, Nirmal, Nizamabad, Jagtial, Rajanna Sircilla, Karimnagar, Peddapalli, Jayashankar Bhupalpally and Mulugu. A Yellow Alert has been issued for heavy rainfall in Bhadradri Kothagudem, Vikarabad, Sangareddy, Medak and Kamareddy districts. Similar warnings remain in force for several northern and western districts on Thursday, while strong surface winds of 30 to 40 kmph are likely across Telangana from Friday onward.
According to the Meteorological Centre, Hyderabad, the weather system is being driven by a Deep Depression that was centred over central Chhattisgarh and adjoining north interior Odisha on Wednesday morning. The system is expected to continue moving nearly westwards across Chhattisgarh and eastern Madhya Pradesh over the next 24 hours. The southwest monsoon trough currently passes through the centre of the Deep Depression, helping sustain widespread rainfall activity across Telangana.
The latest weather observations indicate that the southwest monsoon remains active over Telangana. During the past 24 hours, very heavy rainfall occurred at many places in Jagtial district, at a few places in Mancherial and at isolated locations in Mulugu and Peddapalli districts. Heavy rainfall was also recorded at many places in Kamareddy and Mancherial districts, while several other northern districts, including Adilabad, Nizamabad, Nirmal, Karimnagar, Komaram Bheem Asifabad, Rajanna Sircilla and Warangal, received significant rainfall.
For Hyderabad, the IMD has forecast a generally cloudy sky with light to moderate rain or thundershowers over the next 24 to 48 hours.
